master_output.idea:
**Core idea:** Partition features into the bank's trusted scorecard, raw applicant, and loan-term groups; map ordinal categories to numeric scales and target-encode nominal categories with smoothing/cross-fold to shrink dimensionality; then gate any new feature by both predictive gain AND its feature-importance contribution — not raw accuracy — to surface signals the bank doesn't already use.

**Non-trivial crux:** Target encoding gains efficiency by borrowing the target mean but overfits rare categories, so it requires Bayesian smoothing and cross-fold leakage prevention; and the novelty gate deliberately discards scorecard-correlated predictive power, which only justifies itself if the importance gate is strictly enforced — otherwise you're just rediscovering the bank's own logic.

---

**Research log: data_description.txt summary**

**Target:** `loan_granted` — binary indicator (grant/deny), the decision the model must predict.

**Feature groups from the description:**
- **Trusted scorecard features** (explicitly stated to be used in the bank's scoring): income, debt-to-income ratio, employment duration, credit score, delinquency history, number of open loans, residence type, savings account. These are the foundation — keep them in the base model.
- **Raw applicant features** (not part of the current scorecard): age, employment type (nominal), education level (ordinal), marital status, dependents, property ownership, and the derived `loan_income_ratio`. These are candidates to add selectively.
- **Loan-specific terms:** loan amount, term, interest rate. These may carry signal but could also be redundant with income — test them against the base.

**Categorical semantics to encode correctly:**
- **Ordinals** (education level, employment level): map to a numeric scale so ordering is preserved — e.g. high school (1), bachelor (2), master (3), doctorate (4) — rather than one-hot.
- **Nominals** (loan purpose, employment type): target-encode with smoothing (shrink toward global mean) and cross-fold to prevent leakage — not one-hot — to compress dimensionality.

**Decision discipline:** Every change (add a feature group, switch encoding, apply the gate) gets measured on held-out AUC and the new-feature importance ratio; the gate keeps a feature only if it contributes meaningfully AND isn't scorecard-dominated — preferring novel insight over raw accuracy. Always re-check data types against the description before encoding.

<think>
Okay, let me start by reading the data_description.txt carefully, because any clever trick that ignores the actual feature semantics is just decoration. The description says the target is a binary indicator of whether the loan should be granted, and the key features are a mix: some continuous (income, loan amount), some categorical (education, employment type, loan purpose), and notably a few that are explicitly stated to be "used to compute the scorecard" — let me mark those down as the engineered features the bank already trusts. That last category is the one that keeps bugging me, because the default instinct is to treat all features as equals and let the model pick. But the data description itself is giving me a prior: some features are already part of the bank's own scoring logic. So my first move isn't a modeling trick at all — it's a design decision: don't just throw everything in; partition the features into three groups — (a) the trusted scorecard features the bank already uses, (b) the raw applicant features it doesn't currently score on, and (c) the loan-specific terms (amount, term). I'll keep group (a) in the base model, then selectively add (b) and (c) one at a time, measuring the effect. That way I can say which of the "unused" features actually adds value rather than just overfitting, and whether the loan terms are a real signal or redundant.

Now, the categorical features. The description also mentions some are ordinals (education levels, employment levels) and others are nominal (purpose, employment type). The obvious thing is one-hot, but one-hot swells the dimensionality and throws away the ordering in the ordinals. Here's the leap: take the ordinal categories and map them to a numeric scale so their natural order is preserved — this should help the model treat "high school" < "bachelor" < "master" < "doctorate" as a meaningful progression instead of unrelated buckets. For the nominal categories I'll try target encoding instead of one-hot — replace each category with the mean target rate of that category, which compresses the dimensionality and can capture the signal more efficiently than dummy variables. But I have to be honest about the cost: target encoding is prone to overfit on rare categories, so I'll add smoothing (a Bayesian shrinkage toward the global mean) and cross-fold encoding to prevent leakage, and I'll compare it against one-hot on a held-out set rather than assume it's better.

The second leap is about what NOT to do. The description says the scorecard features are already part of the bank's own logic. So a pure accuracy chase might overfit to patterns the bank already knows — and if I ship a model that only wins by rediscovering the bank's own scorecard, it's not actually adding new value. That reframes the goal: I want the model to be accurate AND to surface signals the bank doesn't yet see. So I'll add a feature-importance gate — only keep a new feature if it contributes meaningfully to the score AND its importance isn't dominated by the scorecard features. This is the part that cuts against the usual "more features, more accuracy" reflex, and it's exactly where I have to be careful, because I'm deliberately excluding some predictive signal in the name of novelty and interpretability.

How do I keep myself honest? I won't declare any winner by intuition. Decision rule: for every change — adding a group of features, switching to ordinal/target encoding — I'll measure AUC and also the new-feature importance ratio on the same held-out set. If a "new" feature's importance is mostly borrowed from the scorecard group, I drop it even if accuracy nudges up — the added-value bar, not the raw bar, is the tiebreaker. And I'll re-check the data types against the description before any encoding step, because a category mislabeled as ordinal is exactly the kind of mistake that silently corrupts everything downstream.

Core idea: Partition features by the bank's own scorecard trust, map ordinals to numeric scales, target-encode nominals with smoothing/cross-fold to shrink dimensionality, and gate new features by both predictive power AND their importance contribution — not just raw accuracy — to surface signals the bank doesn't already use.
Non-trivial crux: Target encoding buys compression at the cost of overfitting rare categories, so it must be regularized with smoothing and cross-fold; and deliberately excluding scorecard-correlated features means trading some accuracy for novel insight, which only pays off if the importance gate is honestly enforced.
